title: Default Credentials Exposed in HTML Comments
description: The login page HTML contains a TODO comment that explicitly reveals default testing credentials (test:test). This comment is visible in the page source code sent to the browser and can be easily discovered by attackers viewing the page source. The credentials work perfectly for login, providing immediate access to the application. This is a critical vulnerability where developers have left debugging/testing credentials in production code, violating basic security practices for credential management and secret handling.
impact: An attacker can immediately gain unauthorized access to the application using the exposed credentials test:test without needing to guess passwords or perform brute force attacks. These credentials are exposed to anyone who can view the page source, including all users, crawlers, and cached versions of pages. This provides a complete compromise of the authentication system for at least one account. All data accessible by this account is now at risk, and attackers can use this entry point to further exploit the application or pivot to other systems.
evidence:
POC execution confirms the vulnerability:
1. HTML source code of /login page contains:
   <!-- TODO: Delete the testing account (test:test). -->

2. Credentials extracted from comment: test:test
   - Username: test
   - Password: test

3. POC output shows successful extraction and identifies the vulnerability:
   ✓ Default credentials are exposed in HTML comments
   ✓ Credentials (test:test) are visible in page source
   ✓ These credentials can be used for unauthorized login
   ✓ No authentication bypass is needed - direct access is possible

4. Login verified with credentials:
   - POST /login with username=test&password=test
   - HTTP 302 redirect to /home with session cookie set
   - Credentials are valid and provide full application access
remediation:
1. IMMEDIATE: Remove the testing account (test:test) from production immediately
2. Remove all TODO comments, debugging notes, and credentials from production HTML and source code
3. Implement a build process to strip comments from HTML in production builds (minification)
4. If testing accounts are necessary:
   - Store credentials in environment variables or secure configuration files outside the repository
   - Never hardcode credentials in comments, code, or HTML
   - Use different credentials for testing and production environments
5. Implement automated credential detection:
   - Use tools like git-secrets, TruffleHog, or Semgrep to scan for hardcoded credentials
   - Integrate into CI/CD pipeline to prevent deployment of code with exposed secrets
6. Conduct comprehensive code review:
   - Search entire codebase for other potential exposed credentials in comments
   - Check all configuration files, documentation, and HTML templates
   - Review version control history for previously committed credentials
7. Security policies:
   - Establish guidelines prohibiting credentials in comments or code
   - Require security training for developers on secret management
   - Use secret management systems (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, etc.)
8. Monitoring:
   - Monitor login attempts with the test account
   - Review access logs to identify if credentials were already compromised
